reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Caused by recurrent gain-of-function mutations in FGFR2 (classically the p.Ser252Trp and p.Pro253Arg substitutions), inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern but usually arising as de novo events linked to advanced paternal age
Bicoronal synostosis produces a turribrachycephalic (tall, flat-backed) skull with a high forehead, midface hypoplasia, proptosis, hypertelorism and downslanting palpebral fissures
The defining limb feature is severe symmetrical bony and soft-tissue syndactyly of the hands and feet, often a 'mitten' or 'sock' fusion involving digits two to four
Midface retrusion narrows the airway and choanae, so obstructive sleep apnoea and feeding difficulty are common and should be screened for early
A cleft or high-arched palate, acne, and hyperhidrosis are frequently seen, and variable intellectual disability occurs
Raised intracranial pressure may develop from the restricted cranial vault or associated hydrocephalus and needs periodic surveillance
Management is multidisciplinary within a craniofacial team, staging cranial vault expansion, midface advancement and hand reconstruction over childhood
Prenatal or postnatal diagnosis is confirmed by FGFR2 sequencing when the phenotype is characteristic
reference.pathophysiology: Apert syndrome results from constitutive activation of fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2). The gain-of-function change increases receptor signalling that normally regulates the balance between proliferation and differentiation in cranial suture mesenchyme and in developing limb tissue. Excess signalling drives premature ossification and fusion of the calvarial sutures (especially the coronal sutures) and disturbs apoptosis in the interdigital tissue, so the digits fail to separate and instead fuse. The same disordered signalling underlies the midface hypoplasia and other skeletal features.
additionalDifferentials: Crouzon syndrome (FGFR2 craniosynostosis without complex syndactyly)
Pfeiffer syndrome (broad thumbs and great toes with craniosynostosis)
Saethre-Chotzen syndrome (TWIST1, ptosis and mild cutaneous syndactyly)
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of FGFR2 to confirm the diagnosis and enable counselling
Cranial CT with three-dimensional reconstruction to map suture fusion and vault shape
MRI of the brain to assess ventricles, hydrocephalus and hindbrain
Ophthalmological review and fundoscopy to detect exposure keratopathy and papilloedema
Polysomnography and airway assessment for obstructive sleep apnoea
Radiographs of the hands and feet to define the syndactyly and skeletal fusions
redFlags: Signs of raised intracranial pressure such as papilloedema, headache or developmental regression
Severe obstructive sleep apnoea or airway compromise from midface hypoplasia
Corneal exposure and ulceration from marked proptosis
reference.prognosis: With coordinated craniofacial, neurosurgical and hand surgery, survival and functional outcomes are good, though cognitive outcome is variable and many children have some degree of learning difficulty. Lifelong follow-up is needed for airway, vision, hearing and intracranial pressure.
pitfalls: Attributing feeding problems or noisy breathing to reflux rather than recognising airway narrowing from midface hypoplasia
Missing raised intracranial pressure because early signs can be subtle in infants
Confusing Apert with Crouzon when the hands are not carefully examined for the characteristic syndactyly
Underestimating the need for staged, lifelong multidisciplinary care
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Perform staged craniofacial surgery: early cranial vault expansion for the bicoronal synostosis to relieve raised intracranial pressure, followed by midface advancement (Le Fort III or monobloc) for the midface hypoplasia
Secure the airway, screening for and treating obstructive sleep apnoea from midface retrusion with CPAP, adenotonsillectomy, midface advancement or tracheostomy as required
Reconstruct the hands and feet with staged surgical separation of the syndactyly to maximise function
Protect vision with ocular lubrication for exposure keratopathy from proptosis, and monitor for papilloedema
Surveil for raised intracranial pressure and hydrocephalus, inserting a shunt when indicated, and repair a cleft or high-arched palate with feeding support
Provide developmental assessment and educational support for variable intellectual disability, together with hearing surveillance
Coordinate a craniofacial multidisciplinary team and offer genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant FGFR2 disorder
